Safe home

Play

For an indoor cat, play isn't just entertainment — it's an outlet for the hunting instinct. Daily 15–30 minute sessions help prevent stress, obesity, and destructive behavior.

Contents

  2. 2. General toy list
  3. 3. Self-entertainment

1

Safety first: choosing materials

Caution

Material matters for toys. Cats play with their paws, but they also take toys into their mouths.

Natural materials: wool, feathers, cotton and linen, jute and sisal, wood.

Synthetic materials: fleece, food-grade silicone, quality ABS plastic.

Avoid cheap plastic with a strong smell (it breaks quickly, has sharp edges, and smells toxic), long fibers and tinsel (threads tear off easily and can cause intestinal blockage if swallowed), and foam rubber (a cat can chew through it, and small pieces get stuck in the stomach).

Small parts: no beads, glued-on eyes, or buttons — a cat can easily bite them off and swallow them, leading to serious gastrointestinal injury.

2

General toy list

Textile and wool:

  • a soft squeaky toy made of cotton/linen;
  • felted balls of 100% wool;
  • fabric mice and fish with no glued-on parts;
  • catnip pouches;
  • plush fleece pillow toys.

Wood and natural fibers:

  • matatabi (silvervine) chew sticks;
  • pressed catnip balls;
  • wooden puzzle mazes;
  • sisal/jute rope balls;
  • scratching posts and mats.

Silicone and rubber:

  • food-grade silicone chew toys;
  • dental massage toothbrush toys;
  • rings made of durable rubber.

Plastic interactive toys (ABS plastic only):

  • multi-level ball-track towers;
  • interactive puzzle feeders;
  • treat-dispensing wobble toys;
  • enclosed plastic balls with a bell.

Toys for play together: wand teasers with fleece ribbons or natural feathers; long textile snake-like cords.

3

Self-entertainment

Puzzle toys and maze feeders keep your cat occupied while you're away. The best motivation is a favorite dry treat.

Examples:

  • puzzle feeders with lids the cat slides open with its paw;
  • the Catit Senses Food Tree;
  • Nina Ottosson puzzle toys of various difficulty levels;
  • interactive treat balls;
  • snuffle mats;
  • peekaboo puzzle boxes.
4

Caution

Caution

Laser pointers: these can cause frustration, since the "prey" can never actually be caught. Always end the game with a real toy the cat can grip and squeeze with its paws.

Ribbons: never leave a cat unsupervised with ribbons or string — there's a risk of choking or swallowing the thread. It's best to keep these stored in closed boxes the cat can't access.

5

The golden rule: supervision

Tip

No toy is 100% safe. Regularly check your cat's toy collection for wear, torn-off parts, or tears. Your attention is the best guarantee of safety.
